summary: Annex 7 sets the registration marks: nationality mark first, a hyphen before a letter, once under the left wing (50 cm high) and on the fuselage or fin (30 cm), characters two-thirds as wide as high, plus a fireproof plate by the door. In the UK an aircraft must be registered, and changes go to the CAA in writing. Part-21 aircraft have a non-expiring CofA kept alive by an annual ARC; non-approved maintenance or modification makes the CofA invalid. Maintenance needs a Certificate of Release to Service, defects go in the tech log, logbooks are kept 2 years after the aircraft goes, and an old weight schedule 6 months.
sections: Registration and Marking of Aircraft (ICAO Annex 7)
Annex 7 sets the minimum standards for displaying nationality and registration marks.
The marks
A group of letters and/or numbers, e.g. G-AGOH, N7207V. The nationality mark comes first. If the registration mark starts with a letter, put a hyphen between them (F-BUDG).
The State of Registry assigns the registration mark.
Where the marks go
Painted on or permanently fixed, kept clean and visible.
Heavier-than-air aircraft:
– once on the lower surface of the wing, on the left half (unless across the whole wing), tops of the letters towards the leading edge, midway between leading and trailing edge
– on both sides of the fuselage between wings and tail, or on the upper halves of the vertical tail (both sides of a single fin)
Balloons: each side, near the widest part. Other lighter-than-air aircraft: visible from the sides and from the ground.
Size and lettering
Lighter-than-air aircraft: 50 cm
Wings of heavier-than-air aircraft: 50 cm
Fuselage or vertical tail: 30 cm
Roman capitals and Arabic numerals, no ornamentation. Each character two-thirds as wide as it is high (except I and 1), solid lines, in a contrasting colour.
Identification plate
A fireproof plate (metal or similar) with the nationality and registration marks, fixed near the main entrance.
Registration in the UK (ANO Articles 24-26, Schedule 4)
In practice you must not fly in the UK unless the aircraft is registered (in the UK or elsewhere) and shows its marks.
Register under the General Classification of Aircraft (ANO Schedule 4).
Owners and part-owners must tell the CAA in writing of any change: ownership, destruction, or permanent withdrawal from use.
Some aircraft need not be registered: non-Part-21 gliders and hang-gliders, and in some cases powered aircraft on test, certification or demonstration flights.
Flying an unregistered aircraft does not excuse any other ANO offence on that flight.
General classification of aircraft
Lighter than air
– non-power-driven: free balloon, captive balloon
– power-driven: airship
Heavier than air
– non-power-driven: glider (including hang-gliders), kite

– power-driven (flying machines): aeroplane (landplane, seaplane, amphibian, self-launching motor glider; includes microlights and powered parachutes), powered lift (tilt rotor), rotorcraft (helicopter, gyroplane)
Airworthiness (ICAO Annex 8; ANO Part 4; UK Basic Regulation)
Annex 8 sets the minimum airworthiness standards that let one State recognise another's Certificate of Airworthiness (CofA).
Since 1 January 2021 EASA rules became UK law (retained, now assimilated law). The old "EASA" and "Annex I / non-EASA" aircraft are now Part-21 and non-Part-21 aircraft.
– Part-21: airworthiness, operations and licensing under the UK Basic Regulation
– non-Part-21: the ANO and British Civil Airworthiness Requirements (BCAR)
Part-21 CofA: non-expiring, kept in force by an annual Airworthiness Review Certificate (ARC). A non-Part-21 CofA (book): issued for 3 years.
The CofA is invalid if the aircraft is modified, repaired or maintained in a non-approved way, and that can also void the insurance.
The Flight Manual (POH) is part of the aircraft's equipment and must be available to the pilot at all times. The CAA may add supplements for aircraft built abroad.
Fly only within the conditions of a valid CofA, e.g. towing a glider needs that approval (ANO Article 87).
No valid CofA but needs to fly (e.g. test flights for a CofA): a Permit to Fly.
Maintenance
Part-21: maintained to an approved aircraft maintenance programme.
Non-Part-21 (not LAA): normally the Light Aircraft Maintenance Schedule (LAMS), with a Certificate of Maintenance Review every 12 months (aircraft under 2,730 kg). The Part-21 equivalent is the ARC.
Owners of Part-21 aircraft need the CAMO's agreement before doing their own maintenance.
Technical Log: flight times, defects and maintenance. Enter a defect before the next pilot flies or at the end of the day, whichever is earlier.

Certificate of Release to Service (CRS): needed, as well as the CofA, after the aircraft or any part needed for airworthiness is overhauled, repaired, replaced, modified or otherwise maintained. Only authorised people may sign it, though pilot-owners may do certain listed minor maintenance (Part-ML / ANGR).
Logbooks: aircraft, engine and (if fitted) variable-pitch propeller logbooks, kept for 2 years after the aircraft, engine or propeller is destroyed or permanently withdrawn.
Temporary loss of airworthiness (Annex 8)
An aircraft not kept airworthy cannot fly until it is restored.

If damaged, the State of Registry decides whether it is still airworthy. If the damage happens abroad, that State may stop the flight but must tell the State of Registry at once; the State of Registry may allow a ferry flight without fare-paying passengers to a repair base.
Mass and balance (ANO Article 43)
The aircraft is weighed and its centre of gravity found; the operator prepares a Weight Schedule. When a new one is made, keep the old one for 6 months.
Flight Manual, limitations and placards (Annex 8)
Limitations go in the Flight Manual, on placards and as instrument markings: loading (masses, CG, floor loads), airspeeds (e.g. VNE, VFE), powerplant, systems and miscellaneous.
Where a limit could be exceeded in flight, the crew must be able to see it on their instruments.
Empty mass usually excludes crew, payload, usable fuel and drainable oil, and includes fixed ballast, unusable fuel, undrainable oil, engine coolant and hydraulic fluid.
Flying outside the CofA or Flight Manual (non-permitted manoeuvres, overweight, CG out) can make the CofA invalid, void the insurance and leave the pilot open to a fine or prison.
Equipment, noise and insurance
Minimum equipment: ANO Schedule 5 (general) and Schedule 6 (radio). Know what your operation needs, e.g. a harness for aerobatics.
Noise Certificate: propeller aeroplanes up to 9,000 kg, all helicopters and microlights, and other subsonic aeroplanes needing more than 610 m to take off.

Insurance: passenger and third-party liability cover is mandatory; hull cover is not, but you could lose a lot without it. Check the certificate is valid for the flight, and watch for excesses, exclusions (unlicensed strips, aerobatics) and pilot warranties (minimum hours). Military aerodromes may need much higher third-party cover.
The PIC is still responsible (ANO Articles 68-69) for a safe and legal flight; insurance does not change that.

cards.q: When is a hyphen used in the marks?
cards.a: When the registration mark starts with a letter (G-ABCD).

cards.q: Where are the marks on the wing?
cards.a: Once on the lower surface, on the left half, tops towards the leading edge.

cards.q: Minimum height of marks on the wing?
Minimum height on fuselage or fin?

cards.a: Two-thirds of its height (except I and 1).

cards.q: What is the identification plate made of and where is it?
cards.a: Fireproof material, near the main entrance.

cards.q: How long is a Part-21 CofA valid?
cards.a: It doesn't expire; it stays valid with a current ARC (yearly).

ref.sec: Airworthiness (ICAO Annex 8; ANO Part 4; UK Basic Regulation)

cards.a: Modification, repair or maintenance in a non-approved way (and flying outside its limits).

ref.sec: Airworthiness (ICAO Annex 8; ANO Part 4; UK Basic Regulation)

cards.q: When is a Certificate of Release to Service needed?
cards.a: After the aircraft or any part is overhauled, repaired, replaced, modified or maintained.

cards.q: Where does a pilot record a defect?
cards.a: In the technical log, before the next flight or the end of the day, whichever is earlier.

cards.q: How long are aircraft and engine logbooks kept?
cards.a: 2 years after the aircraft or engine is destroyed or permanently withdrawn.

cards.q: How long is a superseded weight schedule kept?
Does empty mass include unusable fuel?
cards.a: Yes, and undrainable oil, fixed ballast, coolant and hydraulic fluid; not usable fuel or crew.

cards.q: Is hull insurance a legal requirement?
cards.a: No; passenger and third-party liability cover is.

quiz.q: On a heavier-than-air aircraft, the registration marks on the wing must be at least:
o: 50 cm high, once on the lower surface of the left wing
30 cm high, once on the lower surface of the left wing
50 cm high, on the upper surface of the right wing
30 cm high, on both lower wing surfaces
quiz.why: Wing marks are 50 cm, once under the left half. 30 cm is the fuselage and fin figure.

quiz.q: Each character in a registration mark must be:
o: Two-thirds as wide as it is high (except I and 1)
Half as wide as it is high (except I and 1)
As wide as it is high (except I and 1)
Two-thirds as high as it is wide (except I and 1)
quiz.why: Two-thirds of the height, so the letters aren't stretched. The last option swaps width and height.

quiz.q: A Certificate of Airworthiness ceases to be valid:
o: If the aircraft is modified, repaired or maintained in a non-approved way
Automatically 5 years after it was issued, unless it is renewed by the CAA
When the aircraft leaves its State of Registry on an international flight
At the end of each calendar year, unless a new ARC has been issued
quiz.why: A Part-21 CofA doesn't expire; it stays valid with a current ARC unless non-approved work (or misuse) invalidates it.

ref.sec: Airworthiness (ICAO Annex 8; ANO Part 4; UK Basic Regulation)

quiz.q: A Part-21 aircraft's Certificate of Airworthiness is kept in force by:
o: An Airworthiness Review Certificate, renewed or extended each year
A new Certificate of Airworthiness issued every 3 years by the CAA
A Certificate of Maintenance Review, renewed every 6 months
The pilot's daily inspection, recorded in the technical log
quiz.why: The ARC is the annual check. The 3-year CofA and the CMR belong to non-Part-21 aircraft.

ref.sec: Airworthiness (ICAO Annex 8; ANO Part 4; UK Basic Regulation)

quiz.q: After an aircraft has been repaired it needs, in addition to its CofA:
o: A Certificate of Release to Service
A new Certificate of Registration
A new Noise Certificate from the CAA
A new weight and balance schedule
quiz.why: Any overhaul, repair, replacement, modification or maintenance needs a CRS signed by an authorised person.

quiz.q: A pilot finds a defect during a flight. It must be recorded:
o: In the technical log, before the next flight or by the end of the day if sooner
In the pilot's personal logbook, before the next flight or at the end of the day
On the Certificate of Release to Service, before the aircraft flies again
In the technical log within 7 days, or before the next Airworthiness Review
quiz.why: The tech log records defects; the deadline is before the next pilot flies or the end of the day.

quiz.q: When a new weight schedule is prepared, the previous one must be kept for:
o: 6 months
3 months
1 year
2 years
quiz.why: ANO Article 43: 6 months. 2 years is the logbook period.

quiz.q: Aircraft, engine and variable-pitch propeller logbooks must be kept until:
o: 2 years after the aircraft, engine or propeller is destroyed or permanently withdrawn
2 years after the last entry made in the logbook, whatever later happens to the aircraft
6 months after the aircraft, engine or propeller is sold to a new owner
Until the next Airworthiness Review, when the entries are carried forward
quiz.why: 2 years after destruction or permanent withdrawal. '2 years after the last entry' is the rule for producing a pilot's personal logbook.

quiz.q: The owner of a UK-registered aircraft sells half of it. They must:
o: Tell the CAA in writing
Tell the CAA within 28 days by phone
Re-register the aircraft with new marks
Do nothing; only a full sale needs reporting
quiz.why: Any change of ownership or part-ownership is reported to the CAA in writing.

ref.sec: Registration in the UK (ANO Articles 24-26, Schedule 4)

quiz.q: Which UK insurance cover is compulsory for a private aeroplane?
o: Passenger and third-party liability
Hull cover only, for the aircraft itself
Hull and third-party liability, not passengers
None: insurance is the owner's choice
quiz.why: Liability cover is compulsory; hull cover is optional, though wise.
